facts.text: He died in New York City on February 19, 2018, aged 65. The notice appeared on April 8; that is the publication date, not his death date.
Originally from Toledo, Ohio, he studied at Columbus College of Art and Design, taught drawing at Ohio State University, and moved to New York in 1983.
His LinkedIn profile lists college attendance in 1971–1975.
He worked at Tony Russell Design, founded Designthing, and served as creative director at Campbell Lewis.
His illustration clients included MacWorld, Wired, Playboy, The New York Times, and Harvard Business Review.
He collected contemporary and outsider art, including William Hawkins, Martín Ramírez, Ken Grimes, and Johann Hauser. His obituary connects his illustrations to circus posters and folk art.
Friends knew him as “thing.” He served on the board of St. Andrew’s Golf Club.
A 2017 United Hospital Fund report credits design to Mark Von Ulrich and Maria Kerdel-De Marco.
Pamela, his wife, met him through styling work. Her obituary says they developed Designthing together and supported emerging, contemporary, and outsider artists.
They also collected found and made objects, notably objects depicting hands. The obituary identifies the hand collection as an early interest of Pamela’s.

sections.title: His own account of the digital work

facts.text: In his 2005 email to Robin, he recalled attending art school with Alex Grey, whom he remembered as Alex Velsy.
He dated his introduction to the Macintosh to 1984, through his friend Nilo Rodis, then described buying a Mac and illustrating for MacWorld alongside John Hersey and Scott Baldwin.
He described drawing in an old SuperPaint version, painting in Photoshop, and deliberately preserving pixelation even as publishers favored smoother vector artwork.

research_notes: The hand collection is a useful biographical connection to the recurring hands in the reference images. It does not establish that a particular illustration was inspired by a collected object.
Circus posters, folk art, and outsider-art collecting provide documented context for studying theatrical figures and dense patterning. Any link to a specific symbol remains an interpretation.
An exact birth date, cause of death, and artist-authored explanations of the individual symbols were not established by these sources.
